01 / THE PROBLEM

When a network hides its geometry

Introduction and problem statement

Connections may reveal something about people — even when the features that caused those connections are private, unknown, or impossible to measure directly.

Classical planted clique recovery, the geometric random-graph model and the asymptotic exact-recovery objective.

PART A · THE MODEL

Geometry explains real networks

Imagine a social network. People with nearby homes might meet more often; people with similar interests might follow the same communities. In both cases, being close in some space can make connections more likely. In this research, we study a deliberately simple mathematical version of that idea: a random geometric graph (RGG), where two people connect naturally if their distance is below a fixed threshold.

Why is a geometric model useful?

Physical proximity

In face-to-face contact networks, nearby people have more opportunities to interact. Here distance can literally refer to location.

Similarity and interests

In an online community, closeness may reflect shared interests or behavior rather than a physical location. Such features can be hidden.

Hidden network structure

Devices, accounts, or organizations may connect according to underlying attributes. Their pattern of links can retain clues about those attributes.

PART B · THE MYSTERY

Connections from a hidden group

A coordinated group can connect people who would not normally be linked by the geometric rule. If we knew everyone's hidden positions, those impossible long connections would be obvious. But real positions or personal features may be inaccessible: we observe only who is connected to whom.

One network, three ways to understand it

The same people, with connections added in step 2

What changes? First, we add links between selected people. Then we hide their real positions. In the third panel, the same graph is redrawn from connections alone. The hidden group is no longer marked, and the screen positions reveal nothing about real locations.

A model, not a literal description. Real networks rarely obey an exact distance cut-off, and a coordinated group or botnet need not form a perfect group. This simplified setting isolates a precise question that mathematics can answer.

What are we trying to find? Not just a suspicious link. We want to identify every person in the secretly connected group — with no missing people and no outsiders. This is what we call exact recovery.
WHY STUDY THIS?

An anomaly can hide in plain sight

With the real positions, any newly added connection violates the geometric distance rule and can be detected as unusually long. But if locations or latent features are private, screen distances mean nothing: a graph-drawing algorithm can put nodes anywhere.

Real data may provide only an adjacency list — who follows, communicates with, or connects to whom. Can the structure of those links still reveal a secretly coordinated group?

Botnets and coordinated accounts motivate this kind of question, but the planted group is an idealized mathematical anomaly, not a claim that all such groups form groups.

THE CENTRAL QUESTION

Can a hidden group be recovered using connections alone?

Try the challenge ↓
INTRODUCTION

The planted clique problem

The planted clique problem originates in the study of dense subgraphs hidden within random graphs. In its classical formulation, a graph is first sampled from an Erdős–Rényi model, typically . A subset of vertices is then sampled uniformly, and all missing edges among those vertices are inserted. The computational task is to identify the planted vertex set using the observed adjacency structure only. This line of research goes back to Kučera [1] and the algorithms of Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov [2].

For random geometric graphs, the problem is fundamentally different: edges are dependent through latent positions, and natural cliques are themselves generated by spatial clustering. The question investigated here is whether such dependencies can be exploited to recover the planted clique more effectively than degree ranking alone. We analyze two estimators: vertex degrees (VD) and common neighbours (CN).

The distinction between detection (deciding whether planting occurred) and exact recovery (identifying the selected vertices) is essential: this work studies the latter. See [1–3] and §1 of the paper ↗.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

Problem statement

MODEL · §2

Base model

Let be fixed. Consider the unit -dimensional torus with its periodic Euclidean metric. Its random vertex count is ; conditional on , the latent positions are independent and uniformly distributed on . The parameter is therefore the expected number of vertices.

The hard random geometric graph joins two vertices exactly when their latent positions are within distance . The paper assumes for technical reasons:

The expected degree is , where denotes the volume of the unit ball in dimension . Thus controls the typical number of natural edges incident to a vertex, while controls their geometric length.

All graphical experiments on this page use dimension and periodic boundary conditions. §2 · model definition ↗

MODEL · §2

Planted clique and exact recovery

Fix a sequence of planted sizes . Starting from , choose a set of size uniformly at random and add the missing edges within that set. Pre-existing natural edges are retained, and the observed graph is

Given the observed graph and , but not the latent positions or labels indicating which edges were added, an estimator returns . The goal is exact identification of the originally selected vertices:

One should not confuse the planted set with an arbitrary complete subgraph: a natural clique can exist even in the absence of planting. In particular, planting may add no edges at all. The paper excludes the ill-posed regime together with , where this ambiguity does not vanish.

§2 · planting and recovery ↗

SCOPE · §2

Asymptotics versus finite-size

The theoretical results concern a sequence of Poissonized random geometric graphs: all of , , and may vary, and recovery is assessed as . In contrast, the laboratories and recovery maps generate graphs with exactly vertices, independent uniform positions and a uniformly selected planted set. They are meaningful finite-size experiments, but they do not reproduce Poissonization or directly test asymptotic theorems.

Moreover, certain simulator settings may lie outside the paper's technical assumption . We retain the experiments unchanged and keep this distinction explicit wherever theoretical and numerical results are compared.

WHAT WAS HIDDEN?

Why did we conceal the positions?

03 / FIRST STRATEGY

The VD Algorithm: count connections

Vertex-degree estimator (VD)

When we secretly connect a group, its members gain links. A first idea is to rank everybody by vertex degree — the number of connections they have — and select the top k people.

Degree ordering is computationally cheap; its recovery threshold is governed by the spread of natural vertex degrees.

VD ALGORITHM

How VD works

Degree means the number of connections of a person. The idea: an artificially connected group may give its members unusually high degrees.

1Count the connections of every person.
2Rank people from most to least connected.
3Select the top k people as the suspected group.

VD sees only the links. It never knows the hidden locations or which people were planted.

ALGORITHM · §2.1

Algorithm 1 — VD-algorithm

The degree of vertex in the observed graph is . The estimator returns the vertices of largest observed degree, with a fixed tie-breaking rule:

Algorithm 1 VD-algorithm
Require: observed graph ; planted size
Ensure: estimated set
  1. For every , compute .
  2. Select indices with the largest values among the .
  3. Return .

With degree computation and a size- min-heap, the complexity scale in the paper is . §2.1 · Algorithm 1 ↗

MOTIVATION · §3.1

Why should degree ranking work?

Planting increases the degrees of the selected vertices, but a geometric graph already has natural degree heterogeneity. Let and denote the maximum and minimum degrees before planting. A sufficient condition for success is a strict separation between the smallest observed degree in the planted set and the largest degree outside it:

For an unplanted vertex, the degree cannot increase; a planted vertex gains all within-group edges. Writing for the number of neighbours outside the planted set,

The governing quantities are consequently the natural degree extrema. Assume and write ; its inverse branches and characterize the extrema. With , the paper defines

These scales control the extrema and as the graph grows; the difference therefore naturally appears in the recovery threshold.

WHAT DID WE LEARN?

Big groups can be easier to find.

Planting a group raises the degrees of its members. When the group is large enough, its nodes can move to the top of the ranking — but a small planted group may be lost among naturally popular nodes.

A successful trial is one observation, not a guarantee. Change k, keep the same natural network, and see what changes.

RECOVERY RESULTS · §3.1

Exact recovery and failure

Statements follow the hypotheses and cases of the published theorems; their proofs are located in §5.

POSITIVE RESULT

Theorem 3.1 — VD-algorithm: positive result

Given , the VD-algorithm exactly recovers the planted clique in with high probability in either of the following cases:

(i) Sparse or connectivity regime: and, for any fixed ,
(ii) Dense regime: and, for any fixed ,

The scales and have been defined before the laboratory. §3.1 · Theorem 3.1 ↗

Theorem 3.1 — the positive result⌄

The objective is to establish that every planted vertex has larger observed degree than every unplanted vertex. For , all within-clique edges are present after planting, so . In contrast, the degrees of vertices in do not change. Consequently, a sufficient event is

In the sparse and connectivity regimes, the extremal-degree estimates from §3.1 supply the asymptotic scales and ; a multiplicative margin absorbs their fluctuations, leading to . In the dense regime , both extrema are asymptotically , and their spread is . Hence any linear-in- planted size with a fixed positive coefficient dominates the spread.

This is a sufficient separation argument; it does not imply that VD must fail whenever the displayed inequality is violated. See §5 · proof of Theorem 3.1 ↗.

NEGATIVE RESULT

Theorem 3.2 — VD-algorithm: negative result

The VD-algorithm fails to recover the planted clique with high probability if either:

(i) and, for ,
(ii) , and

These are partial impossibility results for VD specifically. The gap between the positive and negative sufficient conditions is not classified by these theorems. §3.1 · Theorem 3.2 ↗

Theorem 3.2 — the negative result⌄

The negative theorem proceeds by finding an unplanted vertex whose degree outranks a planted one. For sublinear planted size, the maximum natural degree is attained outside the planted set with high probability. The proof therefore compares that extreme against the degree distribution of selected vertices after planting.

For the connectivity-scale case, the natural maximum is of order and typical selected-vertex degrees are near . The assumed upper bound on is insufficient to overcome the gap. A dependence-control argument for the planted vertex degrees then yields at least one planted vertex below the natural maximum.

In the denser case, the proof exploits concentration and fluctuation estimates to show that a perturbation of order cannot separate all planted and unplanted degrees. The argument requires and does not establish a sharp boundary throughout the remaining parameter plane. See §5 · proof of Theorem 3.2 ↗.

04 / SECOND STRATEGY

The CN Algorithm: look for shared neighbors

Common-neighbours estimator (CN)

Counting links ignores their pattern. Two people may share friends: these are their common neighbors. Inspecting how these shared friends connect to one another can reveal a surprisingly specific structure.

Use the full neighbourhood intersection of each observed edge; geometric constraints suppress spurious complete candidate sets.

COMMON NEIGHBORS · EXAMPLE

Meet the common neighbors

Look at the link between u and v. Both are connected to a and b. Other people might connect to only one of them. Can you identify which people are shared?

Click to highlight the two people shared by u and v.

Why might this reveal an anomaly? Natural connections reflect hidden proximity. An added link can bring together people whose shared-neighbor pattern looks very different. CN tests a specific arrangement of shared neighbors rather than just counting links.
CN ALGORITHM

How CN works

CN tests the neighborhood around each observed edge. It never uses locations, degrees alone, or labels that identify the planted group.

1Choose a connected pair (u, v).
2Find their shared neighbors, N(u) ∩ N(v).
3Check that there are exactly k − 2 shared neighbors, and that all k nodes form a group.

Since the edge already contributes two people, a group of size k needs exactly k − 2 additional shared neighbors. CN checks edges until it finds such a group. Many shared neighbors are not enough on their own.

ALGORITHM · §2.2

Algorithm 2 — CN-algorithm

For an observed edge , let denote the set of common neighbours. The algorithm scans observed edges, looking for one whose common-neighbour set contains exactly vertices and itself forms a clique.

Algorithm 2 CN-algorithm
Require: graph ; planted size
Ensure: estimated set
  1. For each observed edge , compute .
  2. If , check whether the vertices in form a complete subgraph.
  3. If they do, return .
  4. If no edge passes both tests, return .

The test on the common neighbours is structural, not merely a count check. Its worst-case scale in the paper is . §2.2 · Algorithm 2 ↗

MOTIVATION · §2.2

Why should common neighbours identify planting?

Let be a natural edge. Its common neighbours are restricted to the lens . Importantly, the diameter of that intersection can exceed . As illustrated in Fig. 1 and §2.2 of the paper, two points in opposite parts of the lens can each be adjacent to both endpoints without being adjacent to one another.

Consequently, a natural edge can have the correct number of common neighbours but still fail the clique-completeness test. By contrast, the planted set is complete by construction; if a planted edge has no extra common neighbours from outside the planted set, it yields the exact estimator .

The proof controls two different error mechanisms: no planted witness is accepted, and a nonplanted edge produces a spurious accepted candidate. This geometric exclusion mechanism can support exact recovery well below the planted sizes required by vertex-degree ranking. §2.2 · geometric motivation ↗

WHAT DID WE LEARN?

Small anomalies can leave strong structural clues.

CN can recover large planted groups, but — at suitable network densities — it can also recognize extremely small ones. Unlike VD, it checks the pattern of shared neighbors, potentially revealing even a group of two people: one planted edge.

This shortcut selects k = 2 and average connections (μ) = 24 to explore a denser network. A successful recovery is not guaranteed: try different densities and random networks.

The k = 2 case below tests whether CN identifies a single inserted edge. This is a finite-size experiment, not a theorem check.

RECOVERY RESULTS · §3.2

Common-neighbours recovery guarantee

Theorem 3.3 provides sufficient conditions, not a full classification of all parameter sequences.

POSITIVE RESULT · THEOREM 3.3

Theorem 3.3 — CN-algorithm: positive result

The CN-algorithm recovers the planted clique with high probability whenever either the first condition holds, for some fixed ,

(3.3)

or one of the following alternatives holds in its respective range:

(3.4)

Here are dimension-dependent geometric constants. The fixed fraction in (3.3) is unrelated to the regime parameter . In particular, the alternative in (3.4) has no conclusion for the intermediate interval .

Conditions (3.3) and (3.4) correspond to the two distinct ways to rule out spurious accepted edges. For appropriate scaling, the guarantees extend to fixed , including . §3.2 · Theorem 3.3 ↗

Theorem 3.3 — witness and false-positive control⌄

A planted edge passes the CN test exactly when its only common neighbours are the other planted vertices. If all planted pairs have at least one additional common neighbour outside , the algorithm can miss the planted set. The paper denotes this obstruction by ; Lemma 6.1 shows that its probability vanishes outside the ill-posed parameter regime.

A separate obstruction is an edge not wholly contained in that passes the test. The proof bounds this possibility by combining two events: the common neighbours form a clique () and their number is exactly (), yielding the decomposition

For , two separated regions inside a common-neighbour lens cannot both contain natural vertices if the common-neighbour set forms a clique. A geometric empty-region estimate produces the exponential term in (3.3).

For , the number of neighbours lying in the lens is controlled using Poisson distributions whose means lie between and . Tail and point-mass estimates give the two conditions in (3.4); the intermediate range is not covered by this sufficient bound. These estimates, combined with a union bound over candidate edges, yield the theorem. See §6 · proof of Theorem 3.3 ↗.

THE TAKEAWAY

Structure can reveal what private locations cannot.

A large enough group can make its members stand out by degree. In other regimes, the pattern of common neighbors provides a different clue, sometimes even for a single planted edge. Which method succeeds depends on network size, density and group size.

The maps estimate success frequencies from repeated simulations. A single run in the playground may succeed in a red region or fail in a green one. That's part of the experiment.
